articles.headline: Even One Drink a Day Raises Your Health Risk. New Study Challenges 'Moderate' Drinking
articles.body: A major new study is upending decades of advice about moderate drinking. Research published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs found that even small amounts of alcohol increase your risk of cancer, heart disease, and premature death. Scientists reviewed over 7,200 peer-reviewed studies and found no level of drinking that provides a net health benefit. The research shows health risks climb with just one drink per day. Bottom line: if you're drinking for your health, you're wasting your time.
articles.takeaway: There's no safe amount of alcohol for cancer risk. If you drink, reducing your intake—even modestly—lowers your disease risk.
articles.source: ScienceDaily / Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs

articles.headline: Tea Cuts Your Heart Disease Risk 11%—But One Habit Undoes It
articles.body: Regular tea drinkers show an 11% lower risk of vascular disease, according to research published in the Journal of Internal Medicine. Black tea showed more consistent benefits than green tea, and moderate-strength brews worked better than weak ones. But here's the catch: drinking tea at scalding temperatures was linked to a 16% higher vascular disease risk compared to non-drinkers. The polyphenols in tea—natural compounds with antioxidant properties—help blood vessels relax and improve blood pressure. The key is letting your tea cool to a sippable temperature before drinking.
articles.takeaway: Drink tea regularly (at least 3 days per week), let it cool to a comfortable temperature, and you may support your cardiovascular health.

articles.headline: Your Brain Can Be Trained to Build Resilience. New Study Shows How
articles.body: A breakthrough study published in Scientific Reports shows that targeted cognitive and emotional training physically rewires your brain to handle stress better. Researchers tracked participants who learned two key emotion regulation strategies: focused attention and cognitive reappraisal. The training produced measurable improvements in how different brain regions communicate—improving your ability to regulate emotions, control attention, and stay mentally flexible under pressure. The neural changes show that resilience isn't something you're born with. It's something you can build through deliberate practice, with visible brain changes appearing after weeks of consistent training.
articles.takeaway: Spend 10-15 minutes daily on cognitive reframing exercises, and your brain will physically rewire itself for better stress resilience within 6-8 weeks.

articles.topic: Ankle mobility knee injury prevention training
articles.headline: Your Ankles Are Sabotaging Your Knees. Here's the Fix
articles.body: Limited ankle mobility is one of the most overlooked drivers of knee injuries. When your ankles can't flex forward properly, your knees and hips compensate by taking on extra load. New research shows that targeted ankle mobility training improves knee biomechanics and reduces injury risk by 20-50%. The solution is simple: add 5 minutes of ankle-focused drills before your workouts. Knee-to-wall rocks, banded ankle mobilizations, and controlled dorsiflexion movements train your ankles to move through their full range. Athletes who add this to their warm-ups show measurably better knee tracking and lower injury rates.
articles.takeaway: Spend 5 minutes on ankle mobility work before training. Focus on knee-to-wall rocks and dorsiflexion drills to prevent knee injuries before they start.
articles.source: NCBI / Journal of Sports Medicine Research

workout.title: Bench Press Strength Block: Max-Effort Horizontal Pressing
workout.tip: Before every heavy bench set, retract and depress your shoulder blades into the bench, plant your feet firmly on the floor, and take your grip — only then unrack. This setup should feel identical every single time.
workout.warmup: 8 min: 10 arm circles forward and back; 10 band pull-aparts; 10 scapular push-ups; 10 dumbbell chest press with light weight (3-sec descent); 1 set × 8 reps barbell bench at 40% 1RM; 1 set × 5 reps at 60% 1RM; 1 set × 2 reps at 72% 1RM — 90 sec rest between buildup sets

exercises.name: Barbell Bench Press
exercises.notes: Touch bar lightly to chest — no bounce. Control the descent for 2 seconds, then press with maximal intent. Drive your feet through the floor and create full-body tension on every rep. Sets 1–2 aim for 5 reps; sets 3–5 hold 3 reps if bar speed drops. Rest 3–4 min between sets — full recovery is mandatory at these loads.

exercises.name: Close-Grip Bench Press
exercises.notes: Grip approximately 16–18 inches apart (just inside shoulder-width). This is a tricep-dominant movement — keep elbows tucked at roughly 45 degrees and feel the triceps fully extend at the top. Load should be approximately 65–70% of your bench press 1RM. Rest 90 sec between sets.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
exercises.notes: Light weight, slow tempo. Lead with your elbows, not your wrists. Stop at shoulder height. This is a shoulder health accessory — not a strength movement. Keep it controlled and avoid shrugging.

workout.cooldown: 7 min: 60-sec doorway or band chest stretch each side; 60-sec cross-body shoulder stretch each side; 60-sec overhead tricep stretch each arm; 60-sec neck side-tilt hold each side; 30-sec thoracic extension over foam roller
workout.description: This push session centers on the barbell bench press at 82–85% 1RM for 5 sets of 3–5 reps, targeting maximal horizontal pressing strength and pectoral, deltoid, and tricep neural recruitment. Close-grip bench follows as a targeted accessory to build lockout strength and tricep hypertrophy, reinforcing the sticking point of the primary lift. This structure is designed for intermediate lifters in a dedicated strength phase.

meal.title: Italian Whole Grain Polenta Bowl with Poached Eggs & Roasted Tomatoes
meal.description: Creamy, buttery polenta made with whole grain cornmeal provides steady carbohydrate fuel, topped with protein-rich poached eggs and sweet roasted cherry tomatoes for a savory Italian-inspired breakfast. Perfect for endurance athletes who want something filling and digestion-friendly before long training days.
ingredients: salt and black pepper to taste
meal.instructions:
1. Preheat oven to 425°F. Toss cherry tomatoes with olive oil, balsamic vinegar, salt, and pepper on a baking sheet. Roast for 15 minutes until blistered.
2. Meanwhile, bring vegetable broth to a gentle boil in a small pot. Slowly whisk in polenta, stirring constantly to avoid lumps.
3. Reduce heat to low and continue stirring for 15–20 minutes until polenta is creamy and pulls away slightly from the pot sides. Stir in butter and Parmesan; season with salt and pepper.
4. Fill a shallow skillet with water, add white vinegar, and bring to a gentle simmer. Create a gentle whirlpool with a spoon, then slide eggs into the center one at a time. Poach 3–4 minutes until whites are set but yolks remain runny.
5. Pour polenta into a bowl, top with roasted tomatoes and poached eggs, and garnish with fresh basil.
meal.tip: Polenta can be made up to 2 days ahead and stored in the fridge; reheat gently with a splash of broth over low heat while you roast fresh tomatoes and poach eggs on race morning. The hot polenta won't spike your blood sugar as hard as simple carbs, making it ideal for sustained endurance.
